apps.localizedDescription:
MuffinEMU is a Wii U emulator for iPhone and iPad (iOS 15 and later), built on Cemu.

- Import games from Files: WUA, decrypted games, and encrypted dumps with your own keys.txt. DLC and updates install from the app.
- Metal renderer by default, with Vulkan through MoltenVK as an option.
- Runs on the interpreter out of the box, and on the faster recompiler when a JIT enabler such as StikDebug is attached.
- An on-screen GamePad laid out from a real Wii U GamePad, with an optional analog stick, skins and a layout editor. Hardware controllers work alongside it.
- Single screen, both screens, or the TV image on an external display.
- Save states, graphic packs, and 31 app icons with matching themes.

This source serves the standard build for SideStore, AltStore and LiveContainer, which re-sign it with your own Apple ID at install.

Bring your own games and keys. No copyrighted content is distributed here.

## Pad presses now animate

Buttons dip under your finger and spring back. The timing is asymmetric on purpose: the
press is a 45ms ease-out, the release is a spring. A spring on the way *down* would make a
button that registered at touch-down **look** like it registered late, which is the exact
complaint this is meant to answer.

Honours Reduce Motion, and there is an **Animate presses** toggle if you would rather they
snap. Nothing about how a control looks at rest has changed.

## Button responsiveness is now a slider

Settings > On-screen Controls. Worth being precise about what it does, rather than shipping
a mystery dial:

**Nothing in the input path delays a press.** The pad reports on `DragGesture`'s `onChanged`
- the first moment a touch exists - and there is no timer anywhere to shorten. A button that
"did not respond" was almost never late. The finger landed just off it, or slid off it
mid-press.

So the slider widens the *target* instead of speeding up a clock that is already instant:
**0-20pt of invisible catchment** outside each button's painted edge. The button looks
identical at every setting; only the area that accepts a touch changes. The row shows the
real number ("+8pt", or "...

## The big one: Single Screen rendered tiny in the corner

Fixed, and it had been there since **v1.0**. `MetalLayerHandle`'s constructor measured
CoreAnimation's current drawable size off the layer and made the implied scale
authoritative. By the time it ran, that number was wrong: the bridge sets the layer's
`contentsScale` to your Render Scale (**Balanced is the default and is half native**), then
the render view enters a window and **UIKit re-asserts the screen's scale**, so the drawable
came out twice the linear size the engine thought the window was. The image was drawn into
the top-left quarter and the rest was cleared black.

Only Single Screen, because the two-screen layouts change size when the layout resolves and
repair it by accident. The fix reads the scale the bridge already wrote instead of measuring
the layer.

**Not yet confirmed on a device.** A free check that confirms or kills it: set Render Scale
to Native and relaunch. If the picture fills the screen there and gets *smaller* on Battery
saver, the diagnosis is right.

## Heat

Measured report: MuffinEMU reached "HOT!". The cause is not subtle - **MuffinEMU runs
three emulated CPU cores, and each one's host thread sits in a reschedule loop that never
sleeps.** On iOS the core's `GetCPUMode()` returns the config value unresolved, and only the
explicit Multicore modes start all three host threads.

## UI consistency pass

A full three-part review audited every screen in the app against its own design
system and found 71 real inconsistencies - not a redesign, just making sure
every screen actually follows the patterns most of the app already established.
Highlights:

- **4 real iPad bugs fixed**: `DecryptROMView`, the DLC/update game picker, the
  Save States sheet, and the account-creation screen were all missing
  `.navigationViewStyle(.stack)`, which meant iPad could render them as a
  two-column split view instead of the intended single screen.
- Every settings row, toggle, and picker now consistently uses the app's real
  row-label font, tint color, and picker style instead of a mix of styled and
  unstyled controls.
- Several screens (Save States, Emulated Devices, the decrypt flow, account

## Reverted: the L3/R3 hit-target change from v2.6

Reported as making on-screen control responsiveness dramatically worse (a
~1.5-2 second hold needed to register at all) - a far more severe problem than
the narrow diagonal-vs-L3 issue it was trying to fix. Every control, L3/R3
included, is back to the same square hit-region they always had before v2.6.

Root-caused this time from an actual device log rather than another guess. The
registered surface was correctly "1366x1024 points, 1.0x scale" - that's Render

its own. The real bug: the code that resizes the Metal drawable to match that
reduced scale never updated the layer's `contentsScale` to match it - so a

honest account rather than just "fixed": the emulated screen was rendering small

## Fixed: Single Screen / Adaptive rendering tiny in the top-left corner

v2.3's Screen Layout port left the emulated screen rendering small, pinned to the
top-left corner, instead of fullscreen - present from the very first launch, not
just after swapping. Root cause: the view showing the TV/GamePad screen is a raw
UIKit view wrapped for SwiftUI, and `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)`
doesn't reliably force a view like that to actually fill the space SwiftUI gives it,
unlike a native SwiftUI view. The fix is to wrap the
view in an inner `GeometryReader` and applying an explicit, measured size instead of
a flexible one - that wrapper was missing here and is now in place. The emulated
screen fills the same space the on-screen GamePad buttons already span.

## What's fixed in this build

- **The whole app freezing when you hit pause** - pausing suspends every guest CPU
  thread under the core's own scheduler lock, and that call was running synchronously
  on the main thread (both from the pause button and from the auto-pause-on-background
  handler). If a guest thread holding that lock was itself waiting on something that
  only resolves once the main thread's run loop is free - a Metal command buffer
  completion handler dispatched back to the main queue is exactly this shape - the main
  thread and the guest thread wait on each other forever: not a slow pause, the whole
  app stops responding to anything, pause button included. Both call sites now run on a
  dedicated background queue instead, so the main thread never blocks on this.
